8.2.9 Mendel’s Laws
Mendel propounded that, among a pair of closely related ‘alleles’ or
factors for a character, only one expresses itself in the first generation as
one of the allele is dominant over the other.
This is so evident that it came
to be called as Mendel’s Law of Dominance.
For expression of each character a pair of factors or alleles are
responsible.
Each one of these alleles is received from each parent.
When
this generation forms gametes, these alleles get separate and each one
enters into a separate gamete randomly.
This separation of alleles at the
time of formation of gametes is called law of Segregation.
Mendel also explained the process of inheritance of more than one
character.
For this, he proposed law of Independent Assortment.
We
will learn more about this in further classes, for the basic understanding
refer in annexure.
Traits that may be passed on from one generation to the next are called
as heritable traits.
We have studied some of them for the pea plant, in the
experiments conducted by Mendel.

parsed_output.answer: Mendel’s monohybrid experiment involved studying the inheritance of a single trait, such as seed color in pea plants. He selected pea plants because they have well-defined traits, are easy to cross-pollinate, and produce offspring quickly. In his experiment, he crossed pure-bred pea plants with yellow seeds (YY) and pure-bred pea plants with green seeds (yy). All the offspring in the first generation (F1) had yellow seeds, indicating that the yellow color is dominant. When these F1 plants were self-pollinated, the second generation (F2) showed a 3:1 ratio of yellow to green seeds. This demonstrated the Law of Dominance, where one trait (yellow) masks the other (green) in the F1 generation, but both traits reappear in the F2 generation in a predictable ratio.
